<x_0.002><y_0.1461>• We have brought this inquiry, then, to an important point. In the article OVERNMENT, we have seen that, unless the people hold in their own hands an efficient power of control on the acts of their government, the government will be inevitably vicious. We have now seen that they cannot override this control to any beneficial purpose, without the means of forming a correct judgment upon the conduct of their representatives.’ We have likewise seen, that one of the means necessary to enable them to judge correctly or the conduct of their representatives, is the liberty to every body of publishing reports of what they do. It remains to injure by what other acts the press can be made to continue to the same desirable end.<x_0.7803><y_0.3078><class_Text>

<x_0.0049><y_0.6813>They who say that no choice ought to be made, say, in effect, that no limit whatsoever ought to be imposed upon the liberty of the press. The one of these propositions is involved in the other. To impose any restraint upon the liberty of the press, is undoubtedly to make a choice. If the restraint is imposed by the government, it is the government that chooses the director of the public mind.
